newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian investment growth seen at risk in 97/98.
newsitem.headline: Australian investment growth seen at risk in 97/98.

text.p: The latest data on Australian investment showed business spending enough to meet the government's lofty target of 16 percent growth in the current fiscal year, but raised a question mark on the outlook for next.

Spending on buildings and equipment rose 6.5 percent in the March quarter in a resounding recovery from the December quarter's 1.6 percent fall. But estimates of what business expected to spend in 1997/98 (July/June) suggested budget forecasts of eight percent growth might be optimistic.
Using a five year average would give growth of just 0.5 percent.
"Whilst we view this as unlikely it does illustrate the risks to the investment outlook for 1997/98," said Maguire.
Morgan's Kyriakopoulos emphasised this was an early estimate and investment intentions may have been curbed by uncertainty ahead of the 1997/98 budget, which was tabled on May 13.
"As it happened the budget was benign and we've had an unexpected cut in interest rates as well -- all of which suggests the next survey will show a better result," he said.
The Reserve Bank cut its official cash rate by 0.5 points to 5.5 percent on Friday.
He also noted investment growth had been in double digits for a number of years and a slowdown would still leave spending at high absolute levels.
Growth of five percent in 1997/98 would produce total spending of more than A$45 billion, almost twice that seen in 1992/93 when the economic recovery was young.

The 6.5 percent rise in investment for the March quarter to A$11.00 billion, in average 1989/90 prices, comfortably topped market forecasts of a 3.5 percent gain and put spending ahead by 18.6 percent on the year.

Expenditure on equipment, plant and machinery rose 5.5 percent, while spending on plant and buildings climbed 8.7 percent. The latter has enjoyed a boom in recent times to be up nearly 42 percent on the first quarter of last year.
Amongst the sectors, the mining industry made the running with investment growth of 15.3 percent on the quarter, but manufacturing and other industries also showed healthy gains.
The overall lift in spending promised to boost economic growth in the quarter with analysts predicting a contribution of 0.4 points or more to expenditure-based Gross Domestic product.
The latest estimate for capital expenditure for all of 1996/97 was A$43.81 billion, some 12.2 percent up on the corresponding estimate for 1995/96.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
"The budget forecast is looking a little on the high side," said John Kyriakopoulos, senior economist at J.P. Morgan.

The second estimate for spending in 1997/98 - the Bureau of Statistics takes seven surveys in all starting two quarters before the financial year in question - showed a rise of just 1.5 percent on the corresponding estimate for 1996/97.
In contrast, the second estimate for 1996/97 had been 22.7 percent higher than the second estimate for 1995/96.
How the intentions turned out in practice was a statistical uncertainty, but the risks seemed stacked on the downside.
"Essentially the government's forecast will require investment intentions to be realised at the same rate as they were in 1995/96," said Societe Generale economist Glenn Maguire.

Investment intentions have turned into actual spending at an increasingly high rate in the last few years to reach a peak in 1995/96 and the same ratio would have to be reached to make the budget forecast of eight percent.
However, the realisation ratio looked certain to have fallen in 1996/97 and if one used a three year average, which analysts felt was reasonable, growth would only be five percent.
